title: No Mastery without the Machine — Medical Education in the Age of Clinical AI
Bridging Brain Connectome and Clinical Notes: A Novel Multimodal Framework for MCI Study.
source: PubMed · IEEE transactions on medical imaging
desc: [IEEE transactions on medical imaging] Integrating brain imaging data with clinical reports enables the effective use of complementary multimodal information, supporting more accurate and timely diagnosis in real-world clinical settings. This approach has gained growing attention in brain disorder research, yet significant limitations remain: how to encode brain structure and function to reflect meaningful neurological patterns, and how to effectively link objective imaging data with subjective text-based reports while establishing interpretable associations. In this work, we propose a novel multimodal framework that aligns brain connectomes with clinical reports in a shared cross-modal latent space at both subject and connectome levels. Our key innovation lies in treating brain subnetworks as tokens rather than raw image patches, enabling more efficient identification of system-level associations between neuroimaging findings and clinical observations. These cross-modal associations are further fused to enhance mild cognitive impairment (MCI) prediction and provide interpretable diagnostic insights. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to integrate both structural and functional brain connectivity with non-imaging clinical information. Experimental validation on the ADNI dataset demonstrates performance competitive with recently reported methods. Notably, despite no explicit connectome-token-level supervision, the learned connectome-text associations recover multiple relationships independently reported in the neuroimaging and clinical literature, suggesting that the framework captures clinically coherent cross-modal associations. This pioneering work advances multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis by bridging the gap between neuroimaging analysis and clinical text interpretation through innovative connectome tokenization and cross-modal alignment strategies.

title: Tele-Cranio: a CT-free AI solution for remote diagnosis and planning of craniomaxillofacial deformities
desc: Computed tomography (CT) is central to craniomaxillofacial (CMF) deformity care, yet dependence on in-hospital imaging constrains remote preoperative assessment and outcome visualization, and repeated imaging can increase radiation and access burdens, particularly for children. We developed Tele-Cranio, a telemedicine-oriented artificial intelligence framework that uses mobile-acquired 2D facial photographs to reconstruct 3D facial morphology, estimate corresponding skeletal morphology and support postoperative facial simulation conditioned on surgeon-defined skeletal plans. Tele-Cranio was developed using 539 paired multimodal samples comprising 2D facial photographs, 3D facial scans and CT-derived skeletal models from individuals aged 3–60 years, including 334 patients with CMF deformities across malocclusion, cleft lip with/without palate, hemifacial microsomia and rare anomalies. Its core model, the Bidirectional Craniomaxillofacial Model-Deformity, learns a shared anatomical representation linking facial soft tissue and skeletal structures across normal and pathological morphology. For remote assessment, Tele-Cranio converts facial photographs into 3D facial surfaces and then infers 3D patient-specific skeletal geometry. For simulation, it generates individualized 3D postoperative facial previews after clinicians complete skeletal planning using standard clinical tools. Validated across heterogeneous CMF subgroups, Tele-Cranio provides an interpretable CT-free layer for remote triage, pre-CT consultation, radiation-free follow-up and surgeon–patient communication, while complementing rather than replacing CT-based definitive diagnosis and operative planning.

title: AI-Assisted Diagnosis: Big Data Analytics in Clinical Decision Support.
source: PubMed · Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)
desc: [Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)] With the development of artificial intelligence (AI), AI-assisted clinical diagnosis, driven by big data analytics and machine/deep learning (ML/DL), has brought great changes in clinical decision. AI enhances disease detection, classification, and treatment planning by processing diverse data such as electronic health records (EHRs), medical images, and genomics. Key applications include high-accuracy cancer screening, neurological disorder prediction, and diagnostics in ophthalmology, endocrinology, and pediatrics. Significant challenges involve data quality/standardization, model interpretability, and ethical/legal concerns. Mitigation strategies include federated learning, Explainable AI, and fairness constraints. Future directions focus on multimodal data fusion, real-time monitoring via wearables, and collaborative human-AI diagnostics. AI is positioned as a tool to augment clinicians, promising improved diagnostic precision, efficiency, and accessibility in precision medicine, contingent on overcoming technical and ethical hurdles through interdisciplinary collaboration.

title: AI-ECG Screening for Early Heart Failure Diagnosis
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Antonio Luiz Pinho Ribeiro; conditions: Heart Failure, Left Ventricular (LV) Systolic Dysfunction; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 5400; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The goal of this parallel-group cluster randomized clinical trial is to evaluate whether opportunistic screening for left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD), using an artificial intelligence algorithm applied to electrocardiograms (AI-ECG), increases the detection of previously unrecognized LVSD among adults aged ≥40 years receiving routine care in primary healthcare centers within the Brazilian Public Health System. LVSD is a key finding in the diagnosis of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), a condition for which effective guideline-directed medical therapies are available but which remains underdiagnosed and undertreated. The study will also evaluate the effects of AI-ECG screening on clinical management, healthcare utilization, implementation outcomes, and healthcare costs. The main questions this study aims to answer are: 1. Does adding AI-ECG screening to usual clinical assessment increase the proportion of patients with newly identified LVSD (left ventricular ejection fraction \<50%) within six months compared with clinical assessment alone? 2. Does AI-ECG screening improve the use of echocardiography, the recognition by primary care teams, and the initiation or optimization of guideline-directed medical therapy for HFrEF? 3. How do LVSD detection rates differ between patients identified through AI-ECG screening alone and those identified through clinical suspicion alone? 4. Is this screening strategy feasible, acceptable, and cost-effective when implemented in primary healthcare? Primary healthcare centers will be randomized to either an intervention group, in which AI-ECG screening results will be provided alongside the standard ECG report, or a control group receiving usual care without AI-ECG results. Participants will: 1. Undergo a routine 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), as clinically indicated by their primary care physician. 2. Be referred for echocardiography based on clinical suspicion of LVSD in both groups or, additionally, a positive AI-ECG screening result in the intervention group. 3. Receive educational materials about HFrEF if newly diagnosed, while participating healthcare professionals will receive educational interventions on heart failure diagnosis and management. 4. Complete questionnaires evaluating educational interventions, when applicable. 5. title: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI
desc: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.

title: The ITE-Transformer: A pre-trained foundation model for predicting individualized treatment effects from electronic health records
desc: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patient's outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients' diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from ~350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients' diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.

title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
desc: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.

title: Modelling Phenotypic Assay Noise for Multivariable Biomarker Discovery using Deep Neural Networks
desc: Accurately predicting cancer drug response remains a major challenge in precision oncology. Although some therapies are guided by clinically-approved biomarkers, these markers often yield limited predictive value and are unavailable for many drugs. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning approaches trained on large-scale cancer cell line pharmacogenomic screens offer a promising route to more comprehensive response prediction, yet they generally assume that phenotypic readouts are measured without error. This assumption is problematic because viability-based drug response assays are inherently noisy, potentially causing models to learn experimental artefacts rather than biologically meaningful determinants of sensitivity. Here, we show that phenotypic measurement noise is present in four widely used cancer cell line screening datasets and introduce Deep Concordance Index Networks (DeepCINET), a deep learning framework that explicitly accounts for this noise. Across datasets, incorporating this noise-aware ranking strategy improves generalization across experimental conditions and to previously unseen samples. DeepCINET outperforms baseline models in multiple settings, with particularly notable gains in prioritizing the most drug-sensitive cell lines. Together, these results establish phenotypic assay noise as a critical and previously overlooked source of error in drug response modelling and provide a principled framework for noise-aware multivariable biomarker discovery.
